description: Chémery is given to Freistroff abbey.
On the last count of Dabo's death, Bishop Conrad leaves Gertrude of Dabo only a life interest in Herrenstein, Turquestein, Sarrebourg and Sarralbe.
Bishop John of Apremont allows the county of Saarbrücken to pass through the female line.
Bishop John of Apremont allows the county of Blieskastel to pass through the female line.
By Hanau's later account, Bitche was exchanged in 1302 for Sarreguemines and Marimont.
Neuviller is pledged to Hanau-Lichtenberg; the bishop of Metz later fails to recover it through the Imperial Chamber.
After John of Geroldseck dies, Bishop Adhémar takes his castle and fiefs back into the bishopric for the time being.
Bishop Dietrich of Boppard rules that fiefs between the upper Saar and Alsace pass only to male heirs.
Bishop Raoul of Coucy lets the Geroldseck fiefs pass through the female line.
Bishop Raoul of Coucy claims that fiefs beyond the Saar revert to the bishopric when a vassal leaves no son.
John of Salm sells his rights as pledge holder of Sarralbe to Henry Bayer of Boppard.
Bishop Conrad Bayer enfeoffs John I of Moers with Sarrewerden, to revert if the male line ends.
John of Fénétrange and the count of Nassau divide the Rosières inheritance along the Saar.
Bishop George of Baden lets the Metz fiefs of the counts of La Petite-Pierre pass through the female line.
Bishop George of Baden reserves Sarrewerden's return to the bishopric should the house of Moers die out.
On George of Ochsenstein's death, the bishop takes his fiefs east of the Saar back into the bishopric.
Childless Sigismund Wecker of Leiningen sells his share of Réchicourt and his Metz fiefs to the bishop.
The bishop grants the Ochsenstein fiefs to Henry of Zweibrücken-Bitsch on the same terms.
Lorraine acquires Blâmont from the bishopric of Metz.
Bishop John of Lorraine declares Sarrewerden returned to the bishopric and enfeoffs his brother Duke Antoine with it.
When John James of Moers dies, the bishop seizes Sarrewerden for Lorraine; Nassau occupies it and the case goes to the Imperial Chamber.
The diet of Augsburg confirms Nassau as owner of Sarrewerden.
Duke Antoine buys the Bayer of Boppard share of Sarralbe, but never pays for it.
The counts of Nassau-Saarbrücken take full ownership of Herbitzheim convent's lands.
The Steinkallenfels give up their rights to Wiesviller, Woelfling, Setting and Dieding.
France occupies Metz and, over the following decades, the bishop's temporal lands.
Bishop Robert of Lenoncourt pledges Hombourg to Philip II of Nassau, keeping the sovereign rights.
Georg Johann I of Veldenz inherits La Petite-Pierre and Lutzelbourg.
When the Siersberg-Dillingen line ends, the duke grants Dillingen to Alexander of Braubach.
Most of Siersberg, a fief for male heirs only, returns to Lorraine.
The Furbach brothers take Calmesweiler in fief from the archbishop of Trier.
Sebastian of Daun grants Eppelborn in fief to Henry of Hagen.
The elector of Trier invests the Dern heirs with the farm of Calmesweiler.
Cardinal Charles of Lorraine invests Count Albert of Nassau with the advocacy of Saint-Avold and the Warndt.
The canonesses of Saint-Pierre of Metz obtain the advocacy of Arriance from the Strombergs in an exchange.
The canonesses of Saint-Pierre of Metz give their Ebersviller property to the Strombergs.
The canonesses of Saint-Pierre of Metz give their Freistroff property to the Strombergs.
Cardinal Charles of Lorraine invests Count Albert of Nassau with Saarbrücken castle, Völklingen and Quierschied.
Lorraine buys the county of Blâmont.
Charles III gives up his claims to the office of Hombourg and Saint-Avold in favour of the bishopric.
Charles III buys Sarralbe, Sarrebourg and Blâmont from Bishop Beaucaire with full sovereignty.
The bishop of Metz cedes Sarralbe to Lorraine (approved in 1609).
Lorraine buys the office of Sarrebourg.
The bishop of Metz cedes Sarrebourg to Lorraine (approved in 1609).
Under the Nomeny agreement the duke takes a third of the dues of Ottonville and Ricrange; the primicerius of Metz keeps the rest and the court.
At Nomeny, France recognises Lorraine's rights over the imperial march of Château-Salins.
The lord of Cronenberg pledges half of Rissenthal.
Charles III orders the return to Mettlach abbey of the electors' arms taken from its church windows.
The dukes receive Blâmont in fief from the Empire (renewed 1609).
Maximilian II makes the Metz fief of Nomeny a marquisate for Nicholas of Vaudémont-Mercœur.
Charles III is invested with the marquisate of Pont-à-Mousson.
John of Hunolstein's Marpingen property is confiscated for misconduct, then returned.
Georg Johann I creates the principality of Phalsbourg with imperial consent.
James of Zweibrücken-Bitsch dies without a son; Philipp V of Hanau-Lichtenberg occupies Bitche.
Georg Johann pledges part of Lutzelbourg to Christian of Savigny and John of Beauvau.
Appeals from Obersteinbach's court now go to Bitche instead of Alsace.
Charles III and the bishop of Metz agree that a quarter of Hellimer belongs to the bishopric.
Nomeny gains judicial and fiscal sovereignty, except appeals and the imperial aid.
Lorraine takes the saltworks of Marsal, Moyenvic and Vic in fief from the bishopric.
The duke joins the county of Bitche to the duchy.
Bitche is joined to Lorraine.
Lorraine's troops occupy the castles and offices of Bitche and Lemberg.
Charles III buys out the Leiningen, Sulz and Hohenlohe shares of Bitche.
The Nancy assizes declare Philipp V of Hanau a disloyal vassal and deprive him of Bitche.
Lorraine occupies Lemberg castle and office, though it was not a Lorraine fief.
Lorraine occupies seven villages of Lemberg as belonging to Bitche.
The bishop borrows from Henry of Guise to redeem the pledge of Hombourg from Nassau.
The bishop grants the castellany of Hombourg-Haut to Henry of Guise as a family fief.
Henry of Guise acquires the castellany of Hombourg-Haut.
Philipp of Furbach sells the Calmesweiler farm to Elisabeth of Dern.
Lorraine and Trier agree how to raise the imperial levy in Merzig-Saargau.
Charles III keeps Insming's provost, mayors and court in their old form.
Nassau marks the bounds of Bouquenom and Sarrewerden with boundary stones; Lorraine protests.
Lorraine and the rhinegrave settle their dispute over Dehlingen, Diemeringen and Rahling.
Dordhal is granted in fief to Nicholas Collet of the Marsal saltworks.
Georg Johann I nearly sells Phalsbourg to France; the sale falls through.
Trier redeems Blieskastel from its pledge to Nassau.
Sebastian of Falkenstein takes the county of Falkenstein in fief from Charles III.
Nassau gives up its claims to Boulay.
Fechingen is to be held in equal halves by the two princes.
The duke obtains the advocacy of Fraulautern convent.
Lorraine obtains the advocacy of Fraulautern convent.
Lorraine gives up high justice and advocacy over Herbitzheim abbey in return for Nassau's rights at Salzbronn.
Lorraine gives up advocacy and high justice over the old Herbitzheim convent lands.
The duke obtains the advocacy of Longeville abbey.
By the treaty of August 1581 with Nassau, Lorraine obtains the advocacy of Longeville abbey.
Lorraine and Nassau drop their claims to the lordship of Lixing.
Lorraine buys the castellany of Hombourg and Saint-Avold.
Lorraine buys most of the castellany of Hombourg-Haut and forms the office of Hombourg-Saint-Avold.
Henry of Guise and his wife sell Hombourg to Charles III; Lorraine takes possession in 1582.
Henry of Guise, after a revoked secret sale to France, cedes the office to Charles III.
An agreement made at Saint-Avold settles the rights of the Kerpen and Nassau at Rouhling.
Lorraine acquires the former lands of Saint-Avold abbey, including the town.
Lorraine obtains the Salzbronn saltworks with firewood rights.
Nassau gives up its overlordship of the Varsberg lands.
Lorraine cedes the advocacy of Wadgassen to Nassau for those of Longeville and Fraulautern.
Lorraine gives up sovereignty and the advocacy over Wadgassen convent.
Calmesweiler is confirmed as a fief of the Dern family.
The emperor forbids the lords of Réchicourt to appeal to the bishop's court; appeals go to the Imperial Chamber.
Hazelbourg village and castle are pledged to Christian of Savigny and John of Beauvau.
Charles III states that appeals to Oberstein's court do not affect Lorraine's sovereignty.
Lorraine's attorney general makes the abbess hand convicts over to the Vaudrevange court.
The Salm sell their share of the Bracs to Charles Philippe of Croÿ.
Georg Johann sells the bailiwick of Phalsbourg to Lorraine, with a four-year buy-back option.
Lorraine buys the lordship of Phalsbourg from Georg Johann I of Veldenz.
Charles III acquires the principality of Phalsbourg.
Lorraine acquires the office of Phalsbourg and Einartshausen with a four-year buy-back option; it pays no general aid.
Bernard of Lutzelbourg marks the boundary of Réding towards Lixheim and Hilbesheim.
The boundary between Nassau-Saarbrücken and the office of Sarreguemines is fixed.
Vergaville abbey's share of the Elviller fief goes to Hans Arnet of Saarbrücken.
Morhange becomes a fief within the German Bailiwick.
Two economic treaties between Trier and Charles III: Merzig-Saargau must buy Lorraine salt only.
Sovereignty over Theley is divided between the duke and the elector of Trier.
Lorraine's officers are told to establish the shares of Lorraine and Trier in Theley's high justice.
Charles III buys Humbert of Eberstein's quarter of Réchicourt and Marimont; the sale is cancelled for non-payment.
The captain of Sarralbe buys boundary stones with Lorraine and Nassau arms for the border with Herbitzheim.
Five boundary stones of the office of Vaudrevange with Lorraine and Nassau arms are recorded.
An inquiry finds that Wiesviller and Woelfling lay within the old bounds of Bitche.
Lorraine acquires the high justice of Coutures from the abbey of Longeville.
Lorraine and Nassau commissioners set twenty boundary stones around Wiesviller and Woelfling.
Charles III arranges to receive the buy-back price for Phalsbourg; the buy-back does not happen.
Charles III pledges Bitche and half of Lemberg to Margrave James of Baden.
The Palatine princes protest in vain against the sale of Phalsbourg.
Charles III pledges his rights in Volmerange to Élisée d'Haraucourt and his wife, keeping the sovereign rights.
Part of Eppelborn passes to Bernard of Löwenstein through his wife, a Hagen heiress.
Marzolf of Braubach sells all his rights in Ippling and Ebring, high justice included, to John of Kerpen.
Marzolf of Braubach sells all his rights in Ippling and Ebring to John of Kerpen.
The duke lifts the confiscation of Ketternostern and Oberstein.
Lixing becomes an imperial fief held directly by the Kerpen.
Zweibrücken's officers seize land and the high justice at Ketternostern.
A boundary stone is set between Sarreguemines and Welferding.
Lorraine acquires the castellany of Marsal from the bishopric of Metz.
The bishop cedes Marsal with its sovereign rights to Charles III in exchange for three villages near Nancy.
Louis of Leiningen-Westerburg takes his newly acquired parts of Réchicourt in fief from the bishop.
The duke allows a gallows at Perl, while ordering the removal of Burgundian salt.
Charles III forbids handing Fraulautern's convicts to Trier and keeps the right to execute or pardon them.
Charles III sells Guenviller, Merlebach and Marienthal to the Haraucourt.
Lorraine buys the fortress and office of Marsal from the bishopric.
At the diet of Regensburg Lorraine agrees to pay 46,000 florins over six years towards the Turkish war.
The bailiwick's officers order Francis of Daun-Falkenstein to let the Eberstein enjoy their quarter of Winterhauch.
The receiver of Bitche reports that the county is not part of the German Bailiwick.
The pledged lands pass to Count Charles of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, who married the margrave's widow.
John George of Helmstatt sells his inherited rights in Insming to the Braubach.
Charles III exempts the 24 aldermen of the advocacy of Saint-Nabor from the general aids.
The Braubachs sell Jean de Schmittberg the ruined castle house of Siersberg, their rights at Büren and Rehlingen and the advocacy of Büren for 1,500 francs.
The Braubachs buy back what they had sold to Jean de Schmittberg within six months.
The Worms chapter seizes Ebring for an unauthorised sale.
The Worms chapter seizes Ippling and Ebring; the case is still open in 1722.
Saarwellingen obtains exemption from half the general aids of 1588–1594.
Charles III buys the Hérange share of the high justice of Insming.

21 November 1598: once the pledgee Charles of Hohenzollern had renounced, Charles III gives the office of Lemberg back to the count of Hanau, keeping Simten, Vinningen, Riedelberg, Erlenbrunn, Staustein, Imsbach and Ranschborn; Lorraine may reoccupy it if no settlement follows.
Francis of Vaudémont becomes count of half the Salm lands (confirmed by the emperor in 1613).
Charles III confirms for ever the privileges and tax freedoms of Hombourg, Saint-Avold and the advocacy villages.
Charles III does homage to the bishop of Metz for Hombourg.
The manorial lordship of Theley passes from the Schmittberg to the Schellart.
Trier and Lorraine jointly survey the bounds of Perl, Apach, Bellmacher and Merschweiller.
Baron Francis of Créhange arbitrates between Charles III and John I of Zweibrücken over Bitche and Hornbach.
A boundary dispute arises at Hüttersdorf.
A survey finds Oberstein within the Empire and the Schaumberg fiefs dependent on Lorraine.
Boundary disputes between Schaumberg and Lichtenberg over four villages.
The elector of Trier invests Bernard of Löwenstein and Charles of Daun with Calmesweiler.
Henry IV of France approves the Marsal exchange.
Lorraine and Zweibrücken agree on how to draw the border of Bitche.
The treaty of Hornbach between Lorraine and Zweibrücken; 25 boundary stones are set.
Lorraine and Zweibrücken settle their common border in detail.
The Imperial Chamber stops pursuing Sarrebourg in Lorraine, having confused it with Saarburg near Trier.
Charles III confirms Vintrange's status as a free allod, exempt from general aids.
Palatine officers mark the bounds of La Petite-Pierre and Lixheim with Fénétrange and Sarreck.
Nassau buys the Varsberg, Stromberg and Löwenstein shares of Güdingen.
The Elector Palatine definitively acquires the lands of Lixheim and Graufthal abbeys.
After the Nomeny treaty, Lorraine still holds part of the Rotte, with no fixed boundary.
The baron of Braubach and John of Zandt sue Lorraine and Trier at the Imperial Chamber over seizures at Honzrath.
The duke restores Insming's court in its old form.
The Nomeny treaty gives sovereignty over Ottonville to the Pays messin.
The principality of Lixheim is surveyed and bounded.
The Nomeny treaty gives sovereignty over Ricrange to the Pays messin.
Luxembourg's attorney general seizes Longeville abbey's revenues at Bambiderstroff.
The castellany of Sarreguemines is pledged as security for buying back Lemberg.
Bernard of Löwenstein takes Eppelborn in fief from the duke of Lorraine.
Frederick IV has Hambach and Roth bounded with stones and marked trees.
Boundary stones are set where Hellering, Bettborn and Oberstinzel meet.
Charles III redeems the pledge of his half of Lemberg, giving the castellany of Sarreguemines as security; completed after the count's death in April 1606.
Bitche's officers extend Lorraine's rights over Altheim's common pasture.
The Imperial Chamber and the Elector Palatine back Philipp Franz of Falkenstein against Eberstein over Winterhauch.
Over 200 boundary stones mark Lorraine's borders with La Petite-Pierre, Hanau-Lichtenberg and Zweibrücken.
Sarrewerden and the lords of Fénétrange bound the Roderbann.
Charles III gives up all rights to Lemberg castle and its district.
Charles III sends the Les Étangs case to the Nancy assizes for good.
Charles III buys Danne and Quatre-Vents, with full justice and forests, from the Lutzelbourg brothers.
Lorraine and Hanau settle Bitche by a treaty arbitrated at Saverne.
The count of Hanau cedes his rights in Bitche to Lorraine.
The Bitche treaty with Hanau; the boundary commission meets and the acts are confirmed in December.
Insming's high court is reformed and its judges reduced to nine.
The powers of Insming's high court are reduced.
Over a hundred boundary stones with the cross of Lorraine and Hanau's arms are set around Lemberg.

Treaty of February and April 1606 with Hanau-Lichtenberg (ratified in December): Charles III renounces the sovereignty and the office of Lemberg-lès-Pirmasens and cedes Vinningen, Simten and other villages; Hanau gives up its claims on Bitche.
After the death of the count of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen in April 1606, the redemption of Lemberg and Bitche is completed and the settlement ratified in December.
Charles III gives up the sovereignty and office of Lemberg-lès-Pirmasens and cedes several villages.
The duke and the elector withdraw the Monclair lords' share of the Saargau's high justice.
Sturzelbronn abbey's records are searched to fix its border with Hanau.
Cardinal de Givry defines the jurisdiction of the bishop's bailiwick of Vic and creates a forestry office.
Luxembourg and the German Bailiwick agree a provisional status quo at Bambiderstroff.
Lorraine and Hanau agree on Bitche; the Imperial Chamber does not approve.
Lorraine reorganises the high justice of Longeville and nearby villages.
April 1607: Charles III orders the governor of Bitche to evacuate the lordship of Lemberg; Lorraine's half leaves the county of Bitche.
An imperial bailiff is arrested at Rahling; the Imperial Chamber's officers are barred from the bailiwick.
Élisée d'Haraucourt founds the new village of Redlach, with the consent of the count of Vaudémont.
The captain of Siersberg has the bounds of his office's high justice confirmed.
Zweibrücken cedes its advocacy over the priories of Zell, Salonnes and Insming.
The Bottenbach district is ceded to Zweibrücken and Hanau.
The count of Réchicourt sues the bishop of Metz at the Imperial Chamber and wins.
Bernard of Löwenstein does homage to Charles III, bringing his imperial lordship into the bailiwick.
Between 1599 and 1608 Francis of Vaudémont buys Turquestein, Saint-Georges, Châtillon and the Donon toll.
The old Meisenthal boundary stone is marked with the year 1608 and three coats of arms.
Frederick IV of the Palatinate creates the imperial principality of Lixheim.
The bailiwick's deputy and Trier's receiver settle the Reimsbach and Oppen disputes using a 1488 court record.
The duke limits the appeals Saint-Avold's court may hear; the townspeople want to answer only to their mayor and aldermen.
Henry II makes the Chamber of Accounts the final court of appeal for Marsal, Dieuze and Sarralbe, ending appeals to Vic.
The Chamber of Accounts rules on appeals, the Kaltenhausen prison and the governor's jurisdiction in Bitche.
A new high court under the first provost replaces the old popular court of Rimling.
The dukes end appeals to the Imperial Chamber from Bitche, the advocacy of Saint-Avold and some Schaumberg fiefs.
The bishopric of Metz gives up Blâmont for good, with the emperor's approval.
Rudolf II invests Duke Henry II with the county of Falkenstein.
Nassau sells the lordship of Helfedange to Pierre-Ernest of Créhange.
Arbitration at Merzig between Lorraine and Oberstein, with Trier and the Palatinate as arbiters, ends without result.
The Imperial Chamber approves the 1581 purchase of Hombourg, saving the bishop's sovereign rights.
Duke Henry II does homage for Hombourg to Cardinal de Givry.
Rudolf II confirms the sale of Sarralbe.
John James II and Philipp III of Eberstein acknowledge Lorraine as overlord for some Schaumberg lands.
An imperial decree lets Henry II treat Phalsbourg-Danne as a free allod, provided he pays the imperial taxes.
Rudolf II confirms Henry II's title of imperial marquis.
The Imperial Chamber and Rudolf II approve the cession of Sarrebourg and Sarralbe.
The Urville conference confirms the rights of the lordship of Raville at Varize.
The Braubach half of Honzrath goes to the commander of Beckingen.
The archbishop of Trier and the duke define their rights in four villages around Hoppstetten.
Anne-Sibylle of Nassau sells her share of Bionville to Pierre Joly.
The Hunolstein sell their share of the Bracs to the rhinegrave Frederick.
Soldiers of the Nancy garrison occupy Mittelbollenbach.
A wayside cross near Besseringen marks the border between the Saargau and Siersberg.
The bailiwick's attorney general forbids the lord of Eppelborn to appeal to the Imperial Chamber.
France takes Chevalin under its protection.
A ducal edict creates a single court for the county of Bitche.
The Vaudrevange assizes allow an appeal to the Imperial Chamber; the attorney general insists it go to Nancy instead.

Commissioners divide the lordship of Berus by lot: the new castle and the second lot go to Jean-Louis de Hohensaxen, the old castle and the first lot to the counts of Metternich; revenues, forests and the mill stay common.
The Chamber of Accounts rules that only the duke holds high justice and the banal rights in the office of Sierck.
Lorraine buys the ban of Delme.
Calmesweiler is sold at auction to the Nancy merchant Mery; Trier protests.
Bernard of Löwenstein's debts force the sale of Eppelborn to Laurent Mery.
Henry II buys the marquisate of Nomeny and the ban of Delme.
Henry II buys the marquisate of Nomeny and the ban of Delme.
Charles Philippe of Croÿ founds the Melkerhof farm near Fénétrange.
Henry II takes the forestry duties away from Hombourg's court, leaving it administrative and judicial work.
The county of Dabo is divided between two Leiningen lines.
With the emperor's consent, the Leiningen-Falkenburg introduce inheritance by the eldest son.
Emperor Matthias renews the Falkenstein investiture.
Salm is recognised as an imperial territory.
George Frederick of Löwenstein buys back part of Eppelborn and does homage to Lorraine.
Three boundary stones with the cross of Lorraine are set at Givrycourt.
Henry II takes Braubach's shares in Lebach and nearby villages in exchange for Fremersdorf.
Lorraine gives Fremersdorf and two villages to William Marcellus of Braubach.
Lorraine acquires two-sevenths of the imperial lordship of Lebach from Braubach.
Matthias confirms Nomeny's separation from the bishopric; Lorraine will sit at the diet as Nomeny.
The castellan of Dieuze sets boundary stones between the ducal woods and those of Nassau and Fénétrange.
The duke confirms Hombourg's rights to firewood and pasture.
Henri II gives Louis de Guise the lordship of Boulay for life; he then styles himself count of Boulay.
The Hahn farm is bought from Braubach and attached to Schaumberg.
The imperial envoy protests against the governor's actions at Vic.
Lorraine's customary law is extended to the office of Hombourg-Haut.
The baron of Créhange's receiver is tried for refusing to recognise Lorraine's sovereignty.
Théding, Rosbruck, Farébersviller and Henriville pass to Louis of Guise.
A court clerk's office is created at Vaudrevange.
Lorraine acquires the Ackerbach farm by exchange.
Sovereignty over Raville passes to Luxembourg, except the Helfedange fief.
February 1615: Henri II sells the mayoralty of Bettingen, redeemable, to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff, captain of Schaumberg.
July 1615: Henri II buys Bettingen back.
Lorraine's officers set boundary stones in the Gering wood.
February 1615: Henri II sells the mayoralty of Limbach, redeemable, to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff, captain of Schaumberg.
July 1615: Henri II buys Limbach back.
Lorraine and the bishop agree that Château-Salins may no longer admit the bishop's subjects as burghers.
The Imperial Chamber overturns a judgment of the bishop's bailiwick of Vic.
The Hornbach agreements give Lorraine sovereignty at Altheim and Beckweiler and a share of Walsheim.
Henri II sells the lordship of Hestroff and Anzeling to André des Bordes, governor of Sierck, for 10,000 francs.
A conference at Marville ends without result.
The houses of Beckweiler are recognised as Zweibrücken's.
On the strength of a 1570 document, Lorraine's attorney forbids the abbot of Freistroff to imprison Chémery's people.
Louis d'Ancerville obtains the right to appoint Bitche's officers.
The count of Réchicourt appeals to the Imperial Chamber against the bishop.
A boundary stone between Haut-Clocher and Langatte bears the Bracs and Col de Cygne arms.
Henri II sells the lordship of Hestroff and Anzeling to André des Bordes, governor of Sierck, for 10,000 francs.
Henry II buys back the Wiltz share of Sarralbe.
Henry II confirms the administrative and judicial autonomy of the office of Sarreguemines.
Sarreguemines accepts the ducal notaries, on condition it belongs to no bailiwick.
Boundary stones are set in the Bisping and Gosselming woods.
A new agreement with Zweibrücken on Bitche's borders.
Créhange is raised to an imperial county within the Upper Rhenish Circle.
The Roderbann is divided between Insviller and Vibersviller.
Homage to the duke for the manorial justice of Gosselming and three other villages.
Diane of Croÿ buys the Landsberg share of the Bracs and of Fénétrange.
Emperor Matthias makes Créhange an imperial county.
George Frederick of Löwenstein acknowledges Lorraine as overlord of Eppelborn and Calmesweiler.
Eppelborn and Calmesweiler are acknowledged as Lorraine fiefs.
The Croÿ brothers make a religious peace with their co-lords at Fénétrange.
The Teutonic Order's grand master asks the Imperial Chamber to intervene at Haustadt.
The duke cedes his rights at Hellimer, Dieffembach and Grostenquin to the Braubach.
Nassau objects to Herbitzheim's criminals being taken to Sarralbe.
Alsweiler is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Bergweiler is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Henry II gives up his right to open Fénétrange castle to his troops.
Henry II gives up his rights in Fénétrange to Charles Alexander of Croÿ.
The commander of Beckingen has a criminal executed with Lorraine's consent, saving the Empire's rights in writing.
Kastel is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Limbach is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Henry II gives up his rights in the Bracs to Charles Alexander of Croÿ.
Marpingen is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Mettnich is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Namborn is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
A 1619 pledge lists the villages belonging to Schaumberg.
A boundary stone with the arms of the Lutzelbourg and of Croÿ separates Réding and Hilbesheim.
At Sarralbe and Sarreguemines, Lorraine and Nassau share out several disputed villages.
Schellenbach is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Sotzweiler is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Thalexweiler is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Tholey is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
Uchtelfangen is among the Schaumberg villages pledged to Jean-Frédéric Freistroff for 18,120 francs.
February 1620: the Conseil d'État maintains the abbot of Freistroff in the middle and low justice against the ducal procurator's claim of 1616.
The co-lords of Merzig-Saargau agree on a joint appeal court.
A higher court is created in Merzig-Saargau to end appeals to the Imperial Chamber.
The barony of Dalem, a fief of Lorraine held by Élisée d'Haraucourt, is made a county.
The duke offers the Eberstein compensation to give up the Hoppstetten fief.
Henry II confirms the abbot of Longeville's right of buffet.
The bailiff levies taxes on the Teutonic Order's free allod of Narbéfontaine.
Same accommodation of July 1620 for the Merzig part of the condominium.
An imperial bailiff is arrested at Puttelange.
The Imperial Chamber rejects a 1564 objection and advises a friendly settlement.
Accommodation of 28-30 July 1620 between Lorraine and Trier confirms undivided joint sovereignty and common justice; approved by Ferdinand II on 4 December 1623.
Lorraine and Nassau buy the Eberstein rights at Setting.
March 1621: Freistroff passes the pledge of Alsweiler to Jean-René de Soetern, with the duke's leave.
March 1621: Freistroff passes the pledge of Bergweiler to Jean-René de Soetern, with the duke's leave.
By his will of November 1621 Henri II leaves Henriette 300,000 francs, secured by a pledge of the county of Bitche.
